title: Why organizations need agile
blurb: Explain why complexity and ambiguity call for agile, and name the problems of traditional delivery that agile addresses.
question: A project finished on time and on budget, yet customers rarely use what it delivered, and its quality problems surfaced only in final testing. Which problems of traditional delivery does PRINCE2 Agile say this shows?

teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile explains the need for agile in terms of complexity. Complex work creates ambiguity, so there is rarely a single perfect solution waiting to be found. Rather than chasing perfection, it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly as you learn what users really need.

The book's Table 2.2 lists problems that traditional, non-agile projects often face. Quality tends to be assessed late in the lifecycle, so chances to fix problems early are missed. Progress is hard to measure without complicated metrics. And projects often focus too much on time and cost, and too little on the benefits and value they are meant to enable.

teach.h: Traditional problems and the agile response
head: Problem (Table 2.2)
What happens
Agile response
rows: Defects found when costly to fix
Check against agreed criteria each iteration
Too much focus on time and cost
Prioritize work by value; release early

teach.h: Predict everything, or learn as you go
Short feedback loops expose problems early
Value, not just time and cost
teach.body: Agile shifts the conversation from 'are we on time and budget?' to 'are we delivering what matters most?'. Teams order their work by value, release usable pieces early and check quality as they go. In PRINCE2 Agile, time and cost are still controlled tightly; the change is that benefits and value get the attention they deserve.

Northmoor Mutual's last mortgage-portal project hit its date and budget, yet applicants abandoned the forms. Defects appeared only in final testing, and board reports showed '80% of tasks complete' without saying what worked. For the next project, manager Halima Yusuf plans two-week iterations with demos to real applicants, orders the backlog by value and reports progress with working increments and burn charts.

teach.text: The book's case for agile is complexity and ambiguity, plus the problems in Table 2.2. Agile is not needed 'to remove governance' or 'to drop the business case'. PRINCE2 Agile keeps both while making delivery adaptable.

items: Complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely one perfect solution.
Better to stay adaptable and able to pivot quickly than to chase perfection.
Traditional problems: quality assessed late; progress hard to measure; too much focus on time and cost over benefits and value.
Agile answers with short feedback loops, working increments and value-based priorities.

summary: You can now explain why organizations need agile: complexity creates ambiguity, so adaptability beats chasing a perfect plan. You can also name the traditional-project problems that agile addresses: late quality checks, hard-to-measure progress and too much focus on time and cost.

A.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, why does complexity make agile valuable?
options: It makes detailed up-front plans far more reliable
It reduces the need for a business case on agile work
It means teams need fewer feedback loops with users
It creates ambiguity, so one perfect solution is rare
A.why: The book says complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely one perfect solution; staying adaptable is better (2.4).

whyNot.0: Complexity makes up-front prediction less reliable, not more.
whyNot.1: All projects still need business justification; complexity does not reduce that need.
whyNot.2: Ambiguity calls for more feedback, not less.

A.q: Which is a problem of traditional projects identified by PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Teams release working products too frequently
Quality is assessed late in the lifecycle
Users are too involved in product reviews
Benefits get more attention than time and cost
A.why: Table 2.2 lists late assessment of quality, which means missed opportunities to fix issues early.

whyNot.0: Frequent releases are an agile strength, not a traditional problem.
whyNot.2: Too little user involvement, not too much, is the usual weakness.
whyNot.3: The book says the opposite: traditional projects focus too much on time and cost and too little on benefits.

A.q: In a complex, ambiguous situation, what does PRINCE2 Agile say is the better approach?
options: Staying adaptable and able to pivot quickly
Searching for the one perfect solution first
Fixing every requirement before starting
Extending each phase until it is complete
A.why: The book says it is better to be adaptable and able to pivot quickly than to hunt for perfection (2.4).

whyNot.1: With ambiguity there is rarely a single perfect solution to find.
whyNot.2: Fixing all requirements up front leaves no room to learn and adapt.
whyNot.3: Long phases delay feedback, which is the waterfall limitation.

B.q: A board cannot tell how far a project has got without a set of complicated metrics. Which traditional-project problem does this illustrate?
options: Progress is hard to measure
Quality is assessed late
Too much focus on time and cost
Benefits are over-prioritized
B.why: Table 2.2 notes that progress is challenging to measure without complicated metrics.

whyNot.1: Late quality assessment is a different Table 2.2 problem, about when defects are found.
whyNot.2: Over-focus on time and cost is a different problem, about what success is judged on.
whyNot.3: The book's concern is the reverse: benefits and value get too little attention.

B.q: According to PRINCE2 Agile, traditional projects often focus too much on which areas?
options: User feedback, rather than plans and schedules
Value, rather than documentation and control
Time and cost, rather than benefits and value
Benefits and value, rather than time and cost
B.why: Table 2.2 says projects often focus too much on time and cost, and less on the benefits and value they are trying to enable.

whyNot.0: Traditional projects tend to under-use user feedback, not over-use it.
whyNot.1: Too much focus on value is not the problem the book describes.

B.q: Which agile practice best addresses the problem of quality being assessed late?
options: Adding a longer test phase at the end of the stage
Reporting the percentage of tasks done each week
Freezing all requirements during initiation
Checking each increment against agreed criteria
B.why: Checking each increment against agreed criteria every iteration finds problems early, while they are cheap to fix.

whyNot.0: A longer final test phase still assesses quality late.
whyNot.1: Percentage of tasks done is the kind of measure that hides real progress and quality.
whyNot.2: Freezing requirements early does not bring quality checks forward.

C.q:
Which two statements are correct, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
1. Complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely a single perfect solution.
2. Traditional projects tend to assess quality early and often.
3. Traditional projects may focus too much on time and cost rather than benefits.
4. Agile is needed mainly to remove project governance.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Complexity breeds ambiguity (1, book 2.4), and traditional projects over-focus on time and cost (3, Table 2.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: traditional projects assess quality late.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: quality is assessed late, and PRINCE2 Agile keeps governance.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: PRINCE2 Agile keeps governance and control throughout.

C.q: At Linfield Outdoor, a project delivered a new ordering app on time and on budget, but customers rarely use it, and its defects surfaced only in final testing. Which two traditional-project problems does this show?
options: Late quality checks and too little focus on value
Late quality checks and too much user involvement
Too much focus on benefits and too little on cost
Easy progress measurement and early testing
C.why: Defects found in final testing show late quality assessment; on time and budget but little used shows time and cost were prioritized over value (Table 2.2).

whyNot.1: Late quality checks fit, but there is no sign of too much user involvement.
whyNot.2: The case shows the reverse: time and cost were met while value was missed.

C.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. In a complex environment it is better to stay [?] and able to pivot quickly than to search for perfection.
options: predictive
adaptable
sequential
documented
C.why: The book says it is better to remain adaptable and able to pivot quickly (2.4).

whyNot.0: Prediction is what complexity and ambiguity make unreliable.
whyNot.2: Sequential delivery is the waterfall pattern that lacks adaptability.
whyNot.3: Documentation does not give the ability to pivot quickly.

reteach.title: Navigating fog
reteach.question: Why does a fixed route plan fail when you cannot see far ahead?

blocks.body: Crossing unfamiliar ground in fog, you do not plot every step at the start. You move a short distance, check where you are, and adjust. Complex projects are the same: ambiguity means the ideal answer is not visible up front. Agile moves in short hops (iterations), checks with users, and changes direction early instead of discovering at the end that the route was wrong.

blocks.text: Remember the three Table 2.2 problems: quality assessed late, progress hard to measure, too much focus on time and cost instead of benefits and value.

explain.body: Complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely one perfect solution. The better move is to stay adaptable and pivot quickly (2.4).

test.q: Why is there rarely one perfect solution on a complex project, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Because the budget is fixed
Because complexity creates ambiguity
Because users disagree about priorities
Because suppliers change their prices
test.why: The book links complexity to ambiguity, which means there is rarely a single perfect solution (2.4).

whyNot.0: A fixed budget constrains a project but is not the book's explanation.
whyNot.2: Disagreement can happen, but the book's reason is ambiguity caused by complexity.
whyNot.3: Supplier pricing is not the reason given in the book.

explain.body: In traditional projects quality is often checked late, so problems that could have been fixed cheaply early are found when they are expensive (Table 2.2).

test.q: What is the effect of assessing quality late, as described in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Lower costs because testing happens once
Faster releases to users
Better-defined benefits
Missed chances to fix issues early
test.why: Table 2.2 says late quality assessment leads to missed opportunities to address quality issues early.

whyNot.0: Late fixes usually cost more, not less.
whyNot.1: Late quality checks delay rather than speed up release.
whyNot.2: When quality is checked has no direct link to how well benefits are defined.

explain.body: Traditional projects often need complicated metrics to show progress (Table 2.2). Agile shows progress through working increments and burn charts (12.4.3).

explain.caption: A burn-down chart: work remaining, visible at a glance.

test.q: Which is a problem of traditional projects according to Table 2.2?
options: Too many working releases to manage each stage
Too much user feedback for the team to process
Progress hard to measure without complex metrics
Benefits and value prioritized above time and cost
test.why: Table 2.2 notes that progress is challenging to measure without complicated metrics.

whyNot.0: Frequent working releases are an agile feature, not a traditional problem.
whyNot.1: Traditional projects tend to get too little feedback, not too much.
whyNot.3: The book says the reverse: time and cost get too much focus.

explain.body: Traditional projects often focus too much on time and cost and too little on benefits and value (Table 2.2). Agile orders work by value and releases early so benefits start sooner.

items.label: where traditional focus tends to sit
what agile puts first when ordering work

test.q: A project celebrates meeting its deadline and budget, but nobody checks whether the expected benefits will appear. Which problem from Table 2.2 is this?
options: Too much focus on time and cost
Quality assessed late in the lifecycle
Progress hard to measure clearly
Too many early releases to users
test.why: Table 2.2 says projects often focus too much on time and cost, and less on benefits and value.

whyNot.1: Late quality assessment concerns when defects are found.
whyNot.2: Hard-to-measure progress concerns status reporting, not the benefits focus.
whyNot.3: Early releases help benefits arrive sooner; they are not the problem.
